verdict: OK to lend in Ranchi engineering & capital goods at or above the 65 threshold, but only to OEM/fabrication units with order visibility and clean safety records; avoid EPC contractors with thin margins and HEC-dependent ancillaries.
title: Ranchi Engineering & Capital Goods: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Ranchi's engineering base is fabrication, castings, transmission structures and EPC work, converting steel and bought-out components into order-bound output.** Cash turns on order execution, not on shelf sales: value sits in the order book and in work-in-progress, and is released only when the client certifies and pays. The city's anchor institutions — HEC, CMPDI and MECON — built this skill pool [2], so the borrower universe is technically strong but institution-dependent. **The data pack gives us no Ranchi-specific output or order-book figure, so collect from customer before you size any exposure.**

## Where cash and value sit
**Working capital is the whole game: receivables and inventory net of payables decide whether growth funds itself or eats the bank [9].** EPC players carry a longer cash conversion cycle than OEMs because execution periods run long [11], and bid and performance bank guarantees tie up limits before a single rupee of revenue arrives [9]. **So when a proposal lands, check the receivable days against the order's payment terms; if retention and milestone billing stretch beyond the stated cycle, ask for the client-wise ageing and the guarantee exposure.** Pricing power is thin — peers show volume growth without margin: Suzlon grew revenue 26% to Rs 4,869 crore in Q2 FY27 while EBITDA stayed near flat at Rs 720 crore and margin narrowed to 14.8% from 18.6% [7].

## What has changed now
**The demand signal is genuinely local: Jharkhand electricity demand is up 15.2% Apr-to-date against India's 9.5%, 5.7 pp faster [D].** Nationally, capital goods output (NIC 28) is up 10.3% YoY and 10.4% Apr-to-date, with exports up 19.8% Apr-to-date in USD [D]. Peer results confirm order flow — DEE's order book crossed Rs 1,300 crore with Q3 revenue up 77% to Rs 286.7 crore [5], and Skipper posted its highest-ever Q2 revenue with PAT up 56% [6]. **But the local news is a safety failure: a worker died at a KDH Projects site in Ranchi when a safety belt snapped at 30 metres [1], and HEC runs at only 20% capacity with 14 engineers leaving this year [3].** Treat both as credit facts, not colour.

## Who to pursue, and how to grow safely
**Pursue OEM and fabrication units supplying power transmission, railway and data-centre demand, and exporters riding the 19.8% export run-rate [D].** Pitti's expansion is backed by order visibility across data centres, mining, off-highway and railways [4] — that is the borrower profile to chase. **Avoid pure EPC contractors with no retention cushion and any unit whose order book leans on HEC.** Structure against the cycle: cash-flow-based limits, monthly stock and receivable statements, and a guarantee sub-limit inside the sanctioned line [9]. Take the order book and client-wise ageing every month, and the safety incident log every quarter.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch receivable days crossing the sanctioned cycle, guarantee utilisation above the sub-limit, and order-book concentration in one client.** A site fatality or safety notice — as at KDH [1] — should trigger a site visit and a hold on fresh disbursal until the contractor's safety compliance is documented. Falling capacity utilisation at an anchor unit, as at HEC's 20% [3], means its vendors' order flow is at risk; ask for their order pipeline before renewing.

Utilisation crosses the sanctioned sub-limit -> seek cash margin or reduce the limit
Quarterly order book and client concentration
Single client above a third of order book -> seek diversification plan or cap exposure
Fatality or safety notice at a borrower site -> site visit and pause disbursal until compliance is documented
Monthly capacity utilisation at anchor units
HEC-type utilisation stays at 20% [3] -> review vendor order pipeline before renewal
